(Only when I sat down to write did I realize how long it has been since my last post here…)

If you have been on Wikipedia lately, you may have noticed a new banner across the top, and for once it isn’t asking for donations:

It announces a contest, organized by Wikimedia, to find a sound logo. Wikimedia runs a whole family of projects, from the famous Wikipedia to Wiktionary, Wikinews and others.

A sound logo, also known as a sound trademark, is a short signature sound for a brand. Here are a few examples that everyone in China knows:

- “Hengyuanxiang, yang yang yang!” (the TV jingle of a knitwear brand, ending in three bleats of the word for “sheep”)

- The QQ message alert: “di-di-di-di-di-di” (QQ being Tencent’s long-running instant messenger)

- Intel: “deng, deng-deng-deng-deng,” as Chinese listeners spell its five-note chime

Do I even need to post the audio? I bet you can already hear them in your head.

The contest’s theme is “The sound of all human knowledge.” Think of the sound of a rocket lifting off, the sound of winning an argument, the sound of Li Bai, the great Tang dynasty poet, writing a poem, or the sound of you studying how Qin Shi Huang, China’s first emperor, unified the six rival states. It sounds wildly far-fetched, but it’s rather fun.

The contest shifts our default way of knowing the world from the eye to the ear, which is good news for those of us who work in acoustics. When it comes to recording something, sound matters just as much as photos. In recent years companies have been taking sound logos more and more seriously. In an earlier article, for example, we described how major carmakers are adding a little seasoning to the sound of their electric vehicles, trying to create a sound logo of their own and make their brand more recognizable.

The electric car of the future: building a brand with sound

Wikimedia is running the contest for the same reason: to make its projects more recognizable. Voice interfaces are everywhere now. When a voice assistant answers a question using Wikipedia, for instance, the user has no idea the answer came from Wikipedia. If Wikipedia had a sound effect along the lines of Intel’s “deng-deng-deng-deng,” users would know where the answer came from. By the same token, if Baidu Baike (the Chinese online encyclopedia run by Baidu) had a logo like “yang yang yang,” users could tell the two apart instantly, and the sound trademark would be doing its job to the full.

Below are a few of the entries submitted so far. I couldn’t begin to guess what any of them is supposed to be, and aren’t they a bit long for a logo…
